title: A push becomes a turn
question: How can an engine make things move?
idea: A push or a pull can change how things move. An engine uses energy to make motion. Its parts work together.

math.title: Little turns add up
math.parentNote: 3 min: count model turns by 2. 9 min: solve and draw. 3 min: explain one strategy. Use tens and ones or a number line. These are pretend engine counts, not real speeds.
math.intro: An engine has a shaft that turns. One turn goes all the way around. Use these pretend counts to solve each problem.
tasks: A model engine turns 24 times, then 18 more times. How many turns in all? Show tens and ones or draw jumps.
The goal is 60 turns. The model has made 42 turns. How many more turns does it need? Show how you know.
Count the model's turns by 2. Fill the gaps: 2, 4, ___, ___, 10, ___, 14, ___, 18, ___.
math.extension: Tell someone: How can 42 + your answer to problem 2 help you check 60 minus 42?

reading.title: The push inside
reading.parentNote: 3 min: preview the three words. 7 min: read together and reread. 5 min: discuss. Help with piston and crankshaft. Point to the story as evidence; spoken answers count.
paragraphs: Jo pushes a toy car away. Leo pulls it back. A push or pull can change its motion.
“What moves a real car?” asks Leo. “Some cars use a gasoline engine,” says Jo. “Let's look at a picture.”
Fuel stores energy. Inside this engine, fuel burns with air. Hot gases spread out and push a part called a piston.
The piston slides inside a tube. A rod links it to a crankshaft. As the piston moves, the crankshaft turns. Other parts carry the turn to the wheels.
“The parts work as a team!” says Leo. The engine changes some of the fuel's energy into motion. Some energy warms the engine and the air.

words.meaning: what can make things move or change
an engine part that slides in a tube
a turning shaft linked to the piston

questions: What pushes the piston? Underline the words that tell you.
How does the piston's motion help the wheels turn? Name two parts in your answer.

writing.title: Tell the motion story
writing.parentNote: 3 min: explain aloud. 4 min: draw and label. 6 min: write 3 short sentences. 2 min: reread. Offer the word bank and frames; accept invented spelling or dictation.
writing.intro: Teach a friend how a gasoline engine makes motion. Write 3 short sentences. Use the story to help you.
writing.draw: Draw a piston, a rod, and a crankshaft. Label them. Add arrows to show motion.
writing.starter: First, fuel ... Next, hot gases ... Then, the parts ...
writing.check: Read it aloud. Did I link fuel, a push, and a turn? Check capitals and end marks.

answers.label: Math · 1
answers.text: 42 turns. For example: 24 + 10 = 34; 34 + 8 = 42. Or combine 3 tens and 12 ones, then trade 10 ones for a ten: 4 tens and 2 ones.

answers.label: Math · 2
answers.text: 18 more turns. Count up: 42 + 8 = 50, then 50 + 10 = 60. Check: 42 + 18 = 60, so 60 - 42 = 18. Accept any sound strategy.

answers.label: Math · 3
answers.text: Missing numbers: 6, 8, 12, 16, 20. Each next count adds 2 turns. The digital model shows pairs up to 20; its counts are not a fuel-use or speed measurement.

answers.label: Reading · 1
answers.text: Hot gases push the piston. Evidence: “Hot gases spread out and push a part called a piston.” Burning fuel with air releases energy; fuel does not push the wheels directly.

answers.label: Reading · 2
answers.text: The piston moves a rod linked to the crankshaft. The shaft turns, and other parts carry the turn to the wheels. Accept a spoken explanation naming at least two linked parts.

answers.label: Writing
answers.text: Example: “First, fuel burns with air. Next, hot gases push the piston. Then, the rod and crankshaft help turn the wheels.” Look for the cause-and-effect chain, three short sentences, labels, and motion arrows.

parentGuidance: This day models a gasoline piston engine, not every engine. A turning crankshaft also pushes and pulls the piston through the rod. The diagram leaves out valves, gears, and timing. Electric cars use motors powered by electricity. Explore with pictures, a toy car, or gestures; keep real engines and fuel out of this activity. Take breaks between sessions.
